info.name: API Platform Demo
info.description:
The WSO2 API Platform demo, end to end. Folders 1-2 set up and publish; folders 3-4 exercise the two demo APIs on the gateway.

* **Folder 1 - API Manager DCR & admin token.** Registers the DCR application and exchanges it for an admin token ({{apim_access_token}}).
* **Folder 2 - API Portal publish.** Mirrors OrderManagementAPI into the Developer Portal's `public` org (README step 2.5), from order-management-dynamic-routing/api-portal/ at the repo root. Deploy it to the gateway first, with the "API Platform Demo - Gateway Management" collection.
* **Folder 3 - OrderManagementAPI.** Header-based dynamic routing + token exchange.
* **Folder 4 - AgentChatAPI.** Header-based, per-org AND per-org-per-use-case token-based rate limiting.

In folders 3 and 4, jwt-auth only authenticates the caller's bearer token -- org identity for routing/rate-limiting comes from the X-Org-Name header, not any JWT claim.

Run '1a' (Railco) and/or '1b' (Acme) in folder 3 to get tokens -- each saves into its OWN variable ({{railco_access_token}} / {{acme_access_token}}), so both can be held at once and every downstream request explicitly uses the right one rather than whichever token was generated most recently.

NOTE: every TLS endpoint here (IS, API Manager, the portal) is self-signed or has an expired cert -- in Postman go to Settings > General and turn OFF 'SSL certificate verification' globally, otherwise these requests fail with a TLS error.

item.name: 1. API Manager - DCR & admin token
item.description:
Registers the Dynamic Client Registration application API Manager needs, then exchanges it for an admin access token. Run 1a then 1b once per API Manager restart -- 1a saves {{apim_client_id}}/{{apim_client_secret}}, 1b saves {{apim_access_token}}, and anything calling an API Manager REST API downstream picks the token up from there.

Ported verbatim (endpoints, body, scopes) from the WK Demo collection's "02 - API Manager - DCR & token" folder; only the variable names differ, to match this collection's `<component>_<thing>` convention.

request.description:
Registers the `publisher_app` DCR application on API Manager, authenticating with the API Manager admin's own basic credentials ({{apim_username}}/{{apim_password}}).

Re-running this is safe: API Manager returns the SAME clientId/clientSecret for a clientName that is already registered, so the test script just re-saves them.

Equivalent curl:
  curl -sk -X POST "$APIM/client-registration/v0.17/register" \
    -u "$APIM_USER:$APIM_PASS" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"callbackUrl":"https://localhost/callback","clientName":"publisher_app","owner":"admin","grantType":"password refresh_token client_credentials","saasApp":true}'

exec: console.log("Saved API Manager admin token to apim_access_token.");

request.description:
Exchanges the DCR app's {{apim_client_id}}/{{apim_client_secret}} (saved by 1a) for an admin access token, via the password grant with the API Manager admin scopes. Saved into {{apim_access_token}}.

Run 1a first -- without it the basic-auth credentials on this request are empty and API Manager answers 401.

item.name: 2. API Portal - Publish OrderManagementAPI
item.description:
README step 2.5: mirrors the freshly-deployed OrderManagementAPI into the Developer Portal's `public` org, so it shows up in the portal catalog alongside the APIs seeded there earlier.

The request uploads the SOURCE OF TRUTH portal artifacts, which live next to the API's gateway definition at the repo root:
  - OrderManagementAPI  order-management-dynamic-routing/api-portal/{api.yaml, definition.yaml}

**Before you run this:**

1. Deploy the API to the gateway first -- "API Platform Demo - Gateway Management" collection, folder 2.
2. Mint a `public`-org admin token and paste it into the {{portal_access_token}} variable:

```
TOKEN=$(ORG_NAME=public ORG_USERNAME=publicadmin ORG_PASSWORD='***' \
  IS_URL=https://is.wso2.com:9444 \
  ROOT_APP_CLIENT_ID=*** ROOT_APP_CLIENT_SECRET=*** ROOT_APP_ID=*** \
  ./scripts/get-org-token.sh)
```

   (The portal's own local-auth login, `POST {{platform_api_base_url}}/api/portal/v0.9/auth/login`, returns a root-org token -- fine for a root-org catalog, not for publishing into `public`.)
3. Postman must be able to read the YAML files off disk: Settings > General > Working directory, point it at this API_Platform_Demo folder and allow access to files outside it. If the file boxes on the Body tab show up empty, re-select the files there by hand -- Postman stores the path, not the contents.

item.name: 2a. Publish OrderManagementAPI to the public org

exec: console.log("Already published to this org -- nothing to do.");

formdata.description: Portal manifest (kind: RestApi, apiVersion api-portal.api-platform.wso2.com/v1). The part's filename MUST be api.yaml -- the portal validates it against an allow-list.
The OpenAPI 3.0 document the portal renders as the API's reference docs.

request.description:
Multipart POST of order-management-dynamic-routing/api-portal/{api.yaml, definition.yaml} -- the same two parts ./scripts/seed-samples.sh uploads for every other bundle, done by hand for the one API the demo adds live.

409 means it is already in this org's catalog; the test treats that as a pass.

Equivalent curl:
  curl -sk -X POST "$API_PORTAL_URL/api-portal/api/v0.9/apis" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    -F "metadata=@order-management-dynamic-routing/api-portal/api.yaml;filename=api.yaml;type=application/yaml" \
    -F "definition=@order-management-dynamic-routing/api-portal/definition.yaml;type=application/octet-stream"

Afterwards, open the Developer Portal's `public` org (https://api-portal.wso2.com:9543/api-portal/public/views/default/) -- OrderManagementAPI is now listed there.

exec: console.log("Saved Railco access_token to railco_access_token collection variable.");

request.description: Requests an application-level access token using Railco's own OAuth2 application (its own client_id/client_secret, and its own token endpoint via {{railco_is_base_url}} in case Railco is served by a different IS instance/tenant than Acme). Fill in railco_client_id / railco_client_secret / railco_is_base_url in the collection variables first. On success, the test script saves access_token into {{railco_access_token}} -- a separate variable from Acme's, so both tokens can be held at once and every Railco-specific request below explicitly uses this one. This token only authenticates the caller; org identity for routing comes from the X-Org-Name header set explicitly on the downstream requests, not from any claim on this token.

exec: console.log("Saved Acme access_token to acme_access_token collection variable.");

request.description: Requests an application-level access token using Acme's own OAuth2 application (its own client_id/client_secret, and its own token endpoint via {{acme_is_base_url}} in case Acme is served by a different IS instance/tenant than Railco). Fill in acme_client_id / acme_client_secret / acme_is_base_url in the collection variables first. On success, the test script saves access_token into {{acme_access_token}} -- a separate variable from Railco's, so both tokens can be held at once and every Acme-specific request below explicitly uses this one. This token only authenticates the caller; org identity for routing comes from the X-Org-Name header set explicitly on the downstream requests, not from any claim on this token.

header.description: Required by the subscription-validation policy on the deployed API. Copy it from the Developer Portal when you subscribe this org's application to the API -- the portal shows it once.

request.description: Calls OrderManagementAPI-v1.0 using {{railco_access_token}} (run request 1a first). jwt-auth verifies the token, then dynamic-routing reads org identity from the X-Org-Name header (not the token) and routes to the matching upstreamDefinitions entry ("railco"). An X-Org-Name value with no matching upstreamDefinitions entry returns 502/503 by design (no fallback map configured); a missing X-Org-Name header returns 503 directly from dynamic-routing.

header.description: Required by the subscription-validation policy on the deployed API. Copy it from the Developer Portal when you subscribe this org's application to the API -- the portal shows it once.

request.description: Calls OrderManagementAPI-v1.0 using {{acme_access_token}} (run request 1b first). jwt-auth verifies the token, then dynamic-routing reads org identity from the X-Org-Name header (not the token) and routes to the matching upstreamDefinitions entry ("acme"). An X-Org-Name value with no matching upstreamDefinitions entry returns 502/503 by design (no fallback map configured); a missing X-Org-Name header returns 503 directly from dynamic-routing.

item.name: 4. AgentChatAPI - Token Rate Limiting
item.description:
Requests 1-3 are Railco-specific ({{railco_access_token}}, run folder 3's request 1a first); requests 4-6 are the Acme equivalents ({{acme_access_token}}, run request 1b first). Each call costs 50 tokens (mock-agent-backend.js returns a fixed X-Completion-Tokens: 50). Limits -- Railco: org=500/min, usecase1=200/min, usecase2=100/min. Acme: org=150/min, usecase1=50/min, usecase2=70/min.

IMPORTANT -- which input picks the rate-limit bucket. The source of truth, agent-chat-rate-limiting/AgentChatAPI-v1.0.yaml, keys its org quotas on `type: header, key: X-Org-Name` -- the **X-Org-Name request header**, matched case-sensitively against ^railco$ / ^acme$. X-Use-Case-Id is likewise a plain header. jwt-auth only authenticates the caller; no token claim feeds the buckets. Same input as OrderManagementAPI's dynamic-routing in folder 3.

If the gateway logs `Rate limit key not found for cost extraction` for every quota and no 429 ever appears, the gateway is still running an older revision of this API that keyed on `authproperty: org_name` -- a client_credentials token carries no org_name, so nothing matched. Re-push it from the source of truth: "API Platform Demo - Gateway Management" collection, request 3c.

NO SUBSCRIPTION KEY: AgentChatAPI carries no subscription-validation policy on the gateway and advertises no subscription plans in the portal -- a valid JWT is the only thing needed to get in, and the advanced-ratelimit token budget is the only thing that limits a caller. The Subscription-Key header these requests used to send has been removed; the gateway neither reads nor requires it here. OrderManagementAPI in folder 3 does not enforce one either as its source-of-truth YAML currently stands -- the Subscription-Key those requests send is accepted but never checked.

request.description: Consumes railco-usecase1-token-budget (200/min) AND railco-org-token-budget (500/min) simultaneously, since org quota has no use-case filter and matches every Railco call. At 50 tokens/call: usecase1 alone allows 4 calls before the 5th is blocked (429, x-ratelimit-quota: railco-usecase1-token-budget) -- click Send 5 times in a row to see it happen.

Consumes railco-usecase2-token-budget (100/min) AND railco-org-token-budget simultaneously. At 50 tokens/call: usecase2 alone allows 2 calls before the 3rd is blocked (429, x-ratelimit-quota: railco-usecase2-token-budget) -- click Send 3 times in a row to see it happen. After running this AND request 1 above to full exhaustion, the org budget has consumed 200 (usecase1) + 100 (usecase2) = 300 of its 500 total -- 200 still remaining, proven by request 3 below.

item.name: 3. Railco org quota STILL has room (different use-case, after 1+2 exhausted)

exec: pm.test("Org quota still had room -- 200 even though usecase1/usecase2 are individually exhausted", function () {

request.description: THE DEMO POINT: X-Use-Case-Id here is "usecase-onboarding" -- a use-case with NO dedicated quota configured, so only railco-org-token-budget (500/min) applies to this call, not any per-use-case limit. Run this AFTER exhausting requests 1 and 2 above (usecase1 and usecase2 both individually blocked at 429). This call still succeeds with 200, proving the org-wide budget still has room (500 - 200 - 100 = 200 remaining) even though both specific use-case quotas are maxed out -- org and use-case budgets are independent, and a 3rd/other use-case is only ever gated by the org-wide ceiling.

Consumes acme-usecase1-token-budget (50/min) AND acme-org-token-budget (150/min) simultaneously. At 50 tokens/call, acme-usecase1's limit (50) is consumed in a single call -- the 1st call succeeds (pre-check 0<50), the 2nd is blocked immediately (pre-check 50 not<50, 429, x-ratelimit-quota: acme-usecase1-token-budget) -- click Send twice to see it happen.

Consumes acme-usecase2-token-budget (70/min) AND acme-org-token-budget simultaneously. At 50 tokens/call: call 1 pre-checks 0<70 (allowed, running total becomes 50), call 2 pre-checks 50<70 (still allowed even though the next deduction overshoots the nominal 70 limit -- running total becomes 100), call 3 pre-checks 100<70 -- false, blocked (429, x-ratelimit-quota: acme-usecase2-token-budget). Click Send 3 times to see it happen. After running this AND request 4 above to full exhaustion, the org budget has consumed 50 (usecase1) + 100 (usecase2) = 150 of its 150 total -- fully exhausted, unlike Railco's org budget which still had room. See request 6 below.

item.name: 6. Acme org quota ALSO exhausted (different use-case, after 4+5 exhausted -- unlike Railco)

exec: pm.test("Org quota is also exhausted -- 429, unlike Railco where it still had room", function () {

request.description: THE CONTRASTING DEMO POINT: unlike request 3 (Railco), this one is expected to return 429, not 200. Acme's usecase1 (50) + usecase2 (70, but only 100 actually consumed before blocking) budgets happen to sum to exactly Acme's org budget (150) -- 50 + 100 = 150. So once both named use-case quotas are individually exhausted, acme-org-token-budget is ALSO fully consumed, and this different/unnamed use-case gets blocked too (429, x-ratelimit-quota: acme-org-token-budget). Run this AFTER exhausting requests 4 and 5 above. This is a deliberate contrast with Railco (request 3): whether the org budget still has headroom after every named use-case is exhausted depends entirely on how the numbers are configured relative to each other -- it is not guaranteed, and Acme's current limits happen to leave zero room.

item.name: 5. LegacyOrderServiceAPI - SOAP behind REST
item.description:
A SOAP Order Management backend exposed as a JSON/REST API. Requests 1x call the SOAP backend DIRECTLY, bypassing the gateway; requests 2x call the same operations through the gateway as REST/JSON. Run a 1x and its matching 2x back to back -- that pairing is the demo.

Deploy the API first with folder 4 of the Gateway Management collection, and start the backend:
  NAME=order_soap_backend PORT=7196 node mock-soap-backend.js

soap_backend_url must be reachable from Postman. It is the backend's own address (default http://localhost:7196), NOT the gateway's.

No token is needed: this API has no auth policy attached.

request.description: The backend's own WSDL, straight from the SOAP service. Proves the backend is up and shows the three operations the API maps onto.
Calls GetOrder as a real SOAP 1.1 client would: a full envelope, with the action in the SOAPAction header. Compare the XML response with the JSON from 2b -- same operation, same backend.
ListOrders takes no parameters. The response holds repeated <ord:Order> elements, which become a JSON array through the gateway (see 2c).
SOAP 1.2 this time: the envelope uses the 1.2 namespace and the action rides inside Content-Type instead of its own SOAPAction header. The backend accepts both versions and picks by content type.

POST /orders maps to the backend's CreateOrder. The gateway sets that operation's SOAPAction, rewrites the path to /OrderService, and json-xml-mediator converts this JSON body into XML on the way out and the SOAP response back into JSON on the way in.

The body mirrors the SOAP envelope because the envelope structure comes from the caller's JSON -- no policy can synthesize it. Use plain unprefixed names: the conversion is not namespace-aware.

Content-Type MUST be application/json or the mediator rejects it with 500.

POST /orders/get maps to GetOrder. A POST rather than a GET because the gateway builds the SOAP envelope from the request body, and a GET has none.

Note OrderId comes back as the JSON number 1001 rather than the string sent: XML is untyped text, so the conversion coerces numeric-looking values.

POST /orders/list maps to ListOrders. The repeated <ord:Order> elements from 1c come back here as a JSON array under Orders.Order. A single result would come back as a bare object, not a one-element array.

An operation the backend does not implement. The backend answers with a SOAP Fault and HTTP 500, and the mediator converts the fault body to JSON like any other response -- so faults stay readable to a REST client.

item.name: 6. ProductCatalogAPI - OData passthrough
item.description:
An OData v4 catalog exposed through the gateway. Requests 1x call the OData service DIRECTLY; requests 2x call it through the gateway.

The contrast with folder 5 is the point: that API needs three policies to transcode SOAP, this one needs NONE. OData v4 is already REST over HTTP with JSON payloads, so the gateway only routes.

Deploy the API with folder 4 of the Gateway Management collection, and start the backend with SERVICE_ROOT pointing at the GATEWAY:
  SERVICE_ROOT=<gateway_base_url>/product-catalog/v1.0 \
    NAME=catalog_odata_backend PORT=7194 node mock-odata-backend.js

Without SERVICE_ROOT the service emits @odata.context and @odata.nextLink URLs pointing at the backend, so a client paging through results would leave the gateway entirely. Compare those URLs in 1c and 2c -- that difference is the demo.

Run 2i before 2j and 2k: it captures the new entity key into odata_last_product_id, which they use.

No token is needed: this API has no auth policy attached.

request.description: The OData service document, straight from the backend: the entity sets it publishes.
The EDMX entity model as XML, straight from the backend.
The Products collection. Look at @odata.context and @odata.nextLink: with SERVICE_ROOT unset they name the BACKEND, which is exactly the URL-leak problem. Compare with 2c.
A single entity by key. OData puts the key in parentheses -- /Products(2), not /Products/2.
The service document through the gateway. Reached by the catch-all operation GET /* -- the API declares no path for it explicitly.

The entity model through the gateway. Worth noting for security review: a catch-all publishes $metadata, so your whole entity model is reachable. Restrict the operations in the API definition if that is not wanted.
The collection through the gateway. With SERVICE_ROOT set, @odata.context and @odata.nextLink now name the GATEWAY -- so a client can follow @odata.nextLink and stay on the gateway. Compare with 1c.

item.name: 2d. Invoke via gateway - Products(2) by key

request.description: Entity by key. Proves the catch-all matches OData's parentheses key syntax, which a plain /{path} placeholder also would.
A navigation property -- TWO path segments after the base. This is the request that proves the catch-all must be /* and not /{path}: a single-segment placeholder returns 404 here.
OData query options need no gateway configuration at all -- they are ordinary query strings and pass through untouched.
@odata.count is the total AFTER $filter but BEFORE $top/$skip, per spec.
Inlines the related supplier into the product, rather than making the client follow the navigation property separately.

exec: // Hand the new entity key to the PATCH and DELETE requests below.

request.description:
Creates a product. Returns 201 with a Location header holding the new entity's URL -- which, like the other embedded URLs, names the gateway only when SERVICE_ROOT is set.

This request's test script captures the new ID into the collection variable odata_last_product_id, used by 2j and 2k.
Partial update of the product created by 2i. ID is immutable and is ignored if sent. Run 2i first, or set odata_last_product_id yourself.
Deletes the product created by 2i. Returns 204 with no body. Running it twice returns 404 -- the second time it is already gone.
